passages.t: Can an unfaithful wife return? Two sisters
passages.happening:
God begins with a question from the law. If a man divorces his wife and she marries another, can he ever go back to her? Would not the land be defiled? Yet Judah has been unfaithful with many lovers, and still speaks of returning (verse 1). There is no high place where she has not given herself to other gods (verse 2). ‘Therefore the showers have been withheld, and no spring rains have fallen’ (verse 3). She calls God Father and friend of her youth and asks if he will be angry forever, while she does all the evil she can (verses 4 and 5).

Then a word from Josiah's days. God asks Jeremiah whether he has seen what faithless Israel has done (verse 6). God thought she would come back, but she did not, and her sister Judah saw it (verse 7). God sent Israel away with a certificate of divorce, ‘Yet that unfaithful sister Judah had no fear’ (verse 8). Judah did not return with all her heart, ‘but only in pretense’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 points to the law of Deuteronomy 24. A man who divorced his wife with a written certificate could not marry her again after she had married another man. Everyone knew the rule. God uses it to show how unthinkable a return should be, and then, in the verses that follow, he offers it anyway.

The spring rains of March and April were needed for the grain to ripen before the dry summer. Baal worship claimed that the storm god controlled the rain. Jeremiah says the missing rain is the LORD's judgment on that very worship.

Verse 6 dates this word to Josiah, who reigned from about 640 to 609 BC. The northern kingdom, Israel, had fallen to Assyria in 722 BC. Josiah's reform cleared away shrines in Judah and reached into the old north, where he destroyed the altar at Bethel. But Judah's return was only pretense: outward changes that did not reach the heart, and after Josiah's death the old ways came back quickly.
passages.later: The law set the rule of verse 1: the first husband ‘may not remarry her after she has been defiled’ (Deuteronomy 24:4). The book of Kings tells of Josiah's reform reaching Bethel (2 Kings 23:15).
passages.hard:
Why does God use such frank sexual language for his people, and does it cast women in a bad light?

The chapter, like Hosea 1 to 3 and Ezekiel 16 and 23, pictures Israel as an unfaithful wife and uses the blunt language of prostitution. Readers rightly notice how uncomfortable this is. Some interpreters, many feminist scholars among them, argue that the picture has shaped harmful views of women and of violence in marriage. Others answer that its target is the whole nation, men and above all the male leaders, kings, priests and prophets, and that the prophets chose the most shocking picture they had to show that idolatry was a betrayal of love.

It must be said plainly. This is a prophetic picture of a city and a covenant. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm a wife, or any woman, and no one may use it to say that a woman deserves to be hurt.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Judah returned, but only in pretense. Ask whether any of your own turning to God has been outward only. And ask what it would look like to return with all your heart.

passages.t: Return, faithless Israel: shepherds after God's heart
passages.happening:
The LORD says that faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than unfaithful Judah (verse 11). Jeremiah is to proclaim toward the north that God calls Israel to return. God will no longer look on them in anger, for he is merciful and will not be angry forever (verse 12). They must only acknowledge their guilt (verse 13).

God calls his faithless children to return. He will take them, one from a city and two from a family, and bring them to Zion (verse 14). ‘Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding’ (verse 15).

In those days no one will talk about the ark of the covenant or miss it, and no one will make another (verse 16). ‘At that time Jerusalem will be called The Throne of the LORD, and all the nations will be gathered in Jerusalem to honor the name of the LORD’ (verse 17). Judah and Israel will walk together again and come home from the north (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The northern kingdom had been in exile for about a century. Jeremiah's call toward the north speaks to those scattered people, perhaps encouraged by Josiah's moves to reclaim the north. The astonishing thing is that the law said return was impossible, and God calls them back anyway.

The word return, shuv, runs all through this chapter and the whole book. It means both turning back to God and coming home from exile.

Shepherds after God's own heart recalls David, called a man after God's own heart. The ark of the covenant was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law. It disappears from the biblical record around the time of Jerusalem's fall. Verse 16 says that in the coming day no one will miss it, because God's throne will be the whole city, and the nations will come to it.
passages.later: Samuel told Saul that the LORD had sought ‘a man after His own heart’ (1 Samuel 13:14). Isaiah saw the same gathering: ‘all nations will stream to it’ (Isaiah 2:2).
passages.asks: God calls the faithless back even when the law said they could not return. Ask whether you have believed there is no way back to God for you. And ask what it means that God's throne would be a whole city rather than a box of gold.

passages.t: God's longing, and a prayer of return
passages.happening:
God speaks of what he hoped for. He longed to make them his sons and give them the best inheritance of all. He thought they would call him Father and never turn away from following him (verse 19). ‘But as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel’ (verse 20).

A voice is heard on the bare heights: Israel's children weeping and begging for mercy because they have forgotten the LORD (verse 21). God calls, ‘Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness’ (verse 22).

Then the people answer. They come to him, for he is the LORD their God (verse 22). ‘Surely the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God’ (verse 23). The shameful god has eaten up what their fathers worked for, even their sons and daughters (verse 24). ‘Let us lie down in our shame; let our disgrace cover us’ (verse 25). They have sinned, they and their fathers, from their youth to this day (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with the words of repentance God longs to hear. It is as though God writes the prayer for his people and hands it to them.

The shameful god of verse 24 translates boshet, shame, a word biblical writers sometimes put in place of Baal's name, as Saul's son Eshbaal is called Ish-bosheth. The prayer admits that Baal worship had eaten up flocks, herds and even sons and daughters, a reference to the child sacrifice condemned elsewhere in the book.

The heights where the people had worshiped other gods become the place where they weep and return. The place of the sin becomes the place of the turning.
passages.later: Hosea gives the people a similar prayer: ‘Bring your confessions and return to the LORD’ (Hosea 14:2). Jesus' story of the lost son has a son who comes home saying, ‘I have sinned against heaven and against you’ (Luke 15:21).
passages.asks: God offers to heal faithlessness, not only to forgive it. Ask what in you needs healing and not only pardon. And ask whether you could pray verse 25 honestly, without blaming anyone else first.
